subject: Legal Studies
name: Legal Studies, Units 3 and 4
about: VCE, Rights, justice and law reform
syllabus: VCE Legal Studies Study Design (from 2024), Units 3 and 4

chapters.title: Principles and rights in criminal cases

points.title: Summary and indictable offences in Unit 3
points.brief: Summary offences are minor and heard in the Magistrates' Court. Indictable offences are serious and may go to trial before a jury.

points.title: Principles of criminal justice
points.brief: The accused is presumed innocent, and the prosecution bears the burden of proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

points.title: Fairness in the justice system
points.brief: Fairness means fair processes, such as an independent decision-maker, a chance to know the case and a fair hearing.

points.title: Equality in the justice system
points.brief: Equality means people are treated the same, and where that would disadvantage someone, measures are taken to correct it.

points.title: Access in the justice system
points.brief: Access means people can learn about their rights and use the justice system to protect them.

points.title: Rights of the accused
points.brief: The right to be presumed innocent, to silence, to a trial without unreasonable delay and to a trial by jury for indictable offences.

points.title: Rights of victims
points.brief: Victims can give evidence in other ways, such as by video link, be told about the proceedings, and be told when the offender is likely to be released.

points.title: Victoria Legal Aid
points.brief: VLA gives free information, advice and, for those who qualify, lawyers for accused people, and helps victims of crime.

points.title: Community legal centres
points.brief: Independent services that give free legal help to accused people and victims, often to those who cannot get Legal Aid.

points.title: Plea negotiations
points.brief: Talks where the accused agrees to plead guilty, often to fewer or lesser charges, saving time and cost but raising concerns about fairness.

points.title: Legal practitioners
points.brief: Lawyers know the law and procedure, prepare and present the case, and help an accused or a victim understand their options.

points.title: Why have a court hierarchy
points.brief: A hierarchy lets courts specialise in cases of different seriousness and lets a party appeal to a higher court.

points.title: Judges and magistrates in criminal cases
points.brief: They manage the hearing, decide questions of law, direct the jury and pass sentence. The parties present their cases.

points.title: Juries in criminal trials
points.brief: Twelve people from the community decide on the facts whether the accused is guilty, and their verdict must usually be unanimous.

points.title: Factors affecting justice in criminal cases
points.brief: Costs, time and cultural differences can stop the criminal system achieving fairness, equality and access.

points.title: Purposes of sanctions
points.brief: Sanctions aim to rehabilitate, punish, deter the offender and others, denounce the crime and protect the community.

points.title: Sanctions and their purposes
points.brief: Fines, community correction orders and imprisonment each serve some purposes better than others.

points.title: Factors in sentencing in Unit 3
points.brief: Judges weigh aggravating factors, mitigating factors, a guilty plea and victim impact statements when they sentence.

points.title: Principles of civil justice
points.brief: The plaintiff bears the burden of proof and must prove the claim on the balance of probabilities.

points.title: Before starting a civil claim
points.brief: A plaintiff weighs costs, whether the time limit has passed, and whether a win could be enforced against the defendant.

points.title: Mediation, conciliation and arbitration
points.brief: In mediation a neutral person helps parties agree, in conciliation they also suggest options, and in arbitration they make a binding decision.

points.title: Consumer Affairs Victoria
points.brief: A government body that gives information and helps settle consumer and tenancy disputes for free.

points.title: The Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal
points.brief: VCAT settles many civil disputes, such as consumer and tenancy claims, more cheaply and quickly than a court.

points.title: Courts in civil disputes
points.brief: A hierarchy of courts spreads civil cases by size and complexity for administrative convenience, and allows appeals.

points.title: Judges, juries and lawyers in civil cases
points.brief: Judges manage the case, including case management to narrow issues, and decide law. A jury of six may decide facts. Lawyers present each side.

points.title: Class actions
points.brief: One claim brought for a group with similar claims, which shares costs and gives access to people who could not sue alone.

points.title: Remedies in civil cases
points.brief: Damages compensate for loss, and injunctions order a party to stop or to do something.

points.title: Factors affecting justice in civil cases
points.brief: Costs and time affect whether the civil system can deliver fairness, equality and access.

units.title: Unit 4: The people, the law and reform

points.title: The Commonwealth Constitution
points.brief: The Constitution sets out how federal parliament is made up, what it may make laws on, and how it shares power with the states.

points.title: The Crown and the Houses of Parliament
points.brief: A bill becomes law only when both houses pass it and the Crown's representative, the Governor or Governor-General, gives royal assent.

points.title: The division of law-making powers
points.brief: Powers are exclusive (Commonwealth only), concurrent (shared) or residual (left to the states). Commonwealth law wins where the two clash.

points.title: Section 109
points.brief: Where a state law and a Commonwealth law conflict, section 109 of the Constitution makes the Commonwealth law win and the state law invalid to that extent.

points.title: A High Court case on law-making powers
points.brief: High Court decisions on what the Constitution allows, such as on Commonwealth tax powers, have shifted power between the states and the Commonwealth.

points.title: The bicameral structure of parliament
points.brief: Two houses must pass a bill. A hostile upper house can block or slow laws, and a friendly one may pass them with little review.

points.title: Other pressures on parliament
points.brief: International treaties and pressure, and the need to reflect the views of voters, shape what laws parliament can and will make.

chapters.title: The Constitution as a check on parliament

points.title: The High Court and the Constitution
points.brief: The High Court interprets the Constitution and protects representative government, striking down laws made outside parliament's power.

points.title: Separation of powers
points.brief: Legislative, executive and judicial powers are held by different bodies, so no one body has too much power.

points.title: Express rights in the Constitution
points.brief: The Constitution protects a few rights expressly, such as the right to trial by jury for Commonwealth indictable offences.

points.title: Courts and statutory interpretation
points.brief: Judges interpret unclear words in an Act when applying it, which can widen or narrow its meaning and becomes precedent.

points.title: The doctrine of precedent
points.brief: Lower courts follow binding precedent from higher courts in the same hierarchy. Other decisions are persuasive, and precedents can be reversed, overruled, distinguished or disapproved.

points.title: Factors affecting courts as law-makers
points.brief: Precedent, judicial conservatism or activism, the cost and time of cases, and the need for standing limit when and how courts make law.

points.title: Courts and parliament
points.brief: Parliament is supreme and can codify or abrogate common law. Courts can still influence parliament through their decisions and comments.

points.title: Why laws change
points.brief: Laws change when society's values shift, new technology arises, or a law no longer works.

points.title: Petitions and demonstrations
points.brief: Petitions show numbers supporting change, and demonstrations draw public and media attention to an issue.

points.title: Courts and law reform
points.brief: Cases can expose problems in the law and push parliament to act, as well as change common law directly.

points.title: The media and law reform
points.brief: Traditional and social media can raise awareness and put pressure on parliament to change the law.

points.title: The Victorian Law Reform Commission
points.brief: An independent body that researches law reform referred by government and makes recommendations. A recent inquiry shows how much it can achieve.

points.title: Royal commissions
points.brief: Inquiries with strong powers to investigate a matter and recommend changes, such as on institutional abuse or aged care.

points.title: Parliamentary committees
points.brief: Groups of members of parliament that investigate issues and recommend law reform.

points.title: Why change the Constitution
points.brief: The Constitution was written in the 1890s, so changes may be sought to reflect new values, rights or ways of governing.

points.title: Changing the Constitution
points.brief: A change must pass both Commonwealth houses, then win a double majority in a referendum: a national majority and a majority in most states.

points.title: What makes a referendum succeed
points.brief: Bipartisan support, public understanding and a clear, simple question make a referendum more likely to pass. Few have.

points.title: The 1967 and 2023 referendums
points.brief: The 1967 referendum passed, counting First Nations people in the census and letting the Commonwealth make laws for them. The 2023 Voice referendum did not pass.
